fact: Dodos were about 63 to 75 centimeters tall. That's roughly up to your waist!
A wild dodo probably weighed about 10 to 17 kilograms (23 to 39 pounds), like a big turkey.
Dodos had grey or brownish feathers.
A dodo had a bare grey head with no feathers on it.
The dodo's beak was green, black, and yellow.
Dodos had strong yellow legs with black claws.
Dodos had a fluffy tuft of curly feathers on their back end, like a little tail.
Boy dodos were bigger than girl dodos and had longer beaks.
The dodo's beak had a hooked tip.
The dodo's top beak was almost twice as long as the part of the skull holding its brain.
Dodos had tiny wings, too small to fly with.
Even though its wings were small, a dodo still had all of its wing bones.
Dodos may have used their small wings for balance and for showing off.
A dodo had a strong neck to hold up its big, heavy head and beak.
Dodos had about six ribs on each side of their body.
Dodo leg bones were thicker and stronger than those of flying pigeons.
Dodos may have been fatter in cool seasons and slimmer in hot seasons.
Each dodo eye had a ring of eleven tiny bones inside it, like other pigeons.
Dodo feathers were most like the feathers of other pigeons.
Scientists think a boy dodo could live to about 21 years old.
Dodos had a big crop, a pouch in the throat for storing food.
Dodos probably lost and regrew their feathers each year. This is called molting.
Dodos molted their wing and tail feathers first.
Dodos held their little wings stretched out, a bit like ostriches and kiwis.
Dodos had a good sense of smell, which may have helped them find fruit.
For its body size, a dodo's brain was about as big as a pigeon's. So dodos were probably about as smart as pigeons!
Scientists studied the shape of dodo brains by making 3D models from their skulls.
A 2026 study suggests dodos may have been most active at dawn and dusk.
Dodos could probably hear low sounds well.
The dodo's top beak could feel a lot, like a sensitive fingertip.
Studies of dodo leg bones show that dodos could run quite fast!
Strong legs helped dodos move quickly through thick forest.
Scientists first studied dodo DNA in 2002.
The dodo DNA scientists studied came from a dodo bone kept in Oxford, England.
Scientists made 3D computer models of dodo skeletons using laser scans.
Parts of the dodo's upper beak could move a little, which may have helped it eat big pieces of food.
The dodo's beak was strong enough to crack hard food.
Scientists looked at thin slices of dodo bones under a microscope to learn how dodos grew.
Dodo chicks probably grew up very fast.
Scientists once named a fruit fly gene 'dodo' because it is needed for flying.
A spider from Mauritius was named after the dodo: Nephilengys dodo.
Two kinds of ants from Mauritius were named after the dodo.
A tiny sea creature from a coral reef near Réunion is named Hansenium dodo.
The dodo was a kind of pigeon!
The dodo belonged to the same bird family as pigeons and doves.
The dodo's closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon.
The Nicobar pigeon lives on small islands in Asia, from India to the Solomon Islands.
The dodo's closest relative of all was the Rodrigues solitaire, another big bird that couldn't fly.
The Rodrigues solitaire lived on the island of Rodrigues, near Mauritius.
The Rodrigues solitaire is also extinct.
Rodrigues solitaires had bony knobs on their wings that they used to fight.
Like the dodo, the Rodrigues solitaire laid just one egg at a time.
Crowned pigeons from New Guinea are also close cousins of the dodo.
The tooth-billed pigeon of Samoa has a beak that looks a bit like a dodo's.
The dodo's ancestors could fly. They probably flew to the islands, island by island, from Asia.
The ancestors of the dodo and the solitaire split apart about 23 million years ago.
Another giant pigeon that couldn't fly once lived in Fiji. It was only a little smaller than the dodo.
Long ago, scientists guessed the dodo was a small ostrich, a vulture, or an albatross. They were wrong!
In 1842, a Danish scientist named Johannes Reinhardt said dodos were ground pigeons. People laughed, but he was right!
Dodo leg bones have features found only in pigeons.
Like other pigeons, dodos had bare skin around their eyes.
Dodos ate fruit that fell from trees.
Dodos probably also ate nuts, seeds, bulbs, and roots.
Some scientists think dodos might have eaten crabs and shellfish too.
Dodos swallowed stones to help grind up food in their stomachs. These are called gizzard stones.
In 1638, a man in London watched a dodo eat pebbles as big as nutmegs!
A letter from 1631 says the dodo's food was 'raw fruit.'
That 1631 letter was lost for a long time and was found again in 2017.
Dodos may have stuffed themselves with ripe fruit before the dry season, when food was hard to find.
A scientist from Mauritius thought dodos mostly ate palm fruits.
Old reports say dodos had big, greedy appetites.
Dodo chicks may have been fed 'crop milk,' a special food that pigeon parents make.
Dodos probably liked big seeds and big fruits.
Dodos helped plants grow by spreading their seeds around.
Dodos could only reach food near the ground, because they couldn't fly up into trees.
There is a tree called the 'dodo tree,' or tambalacoque. It grows only on Mauritius.
The dodo tree's fruit is a bit like a peach, with a hard pit inside.
Dodo tree flowers and fruit grow right on the trunk and branches.
Some people thought dodo tree seeds could only sprout after a dodo ate them. That turned out to be wrong: the seeds can sprout without dodos.
The dodo tree has no growth rings, so it's hard to tell how old one is.
A dodo laid just one egg at a time.
Dodos probably built their nests on the ground.
One old report says the dodo egg was white.
Scientists think dodos laid eggs around August.
Dodo chicks grew almost to adult size before the stormy cyclone season.
Dodo parents probably took care of their chicks for a long time.
Bones of baby dodos are very rare. Only one has ever been found, and it is now lost.
A museum in South Africa has an egg that some say is a dodo egg, but it might be an ostrich egg.
One old writer said dodos sounded like a baby goose.
Dodos lived only on one island: Mauritius.
Mauritius is an island in the Indian Ocean, east of Madagascar.
Mauritius is about 2,000 kilometers (1,300 miles) from the coast of Africa.
Mauritius, Réunion, and Rodrigues are called the Mascarene Islands.
The Mascarene Islands were made by volcanoes.
The Mascarene Islands are less than 10 million years old.
Before people came, Mauritius was covered in forest.
Dodos probably lived in the woods near the drier coasts of Mauritius.
Dodo bones have also been found in caves up in the mountains.
There were no big hunting animals on Mauritius before people came, so dodos had nothing to run from.
Dodos had lots of food and no predators, so they didn't need to fly.
The capital city of Mauritius is Port Louis.
Mauritius was named after Prince Maurice, a Dutch prince.
Dodos shared their island with giant tortoises that are now extinct too.
The red rail was another bird from Mauritius that couldn't fly. It is extinct too.
The broad-billed parrot lived on Mauritius with the dodo.
A dodo is on the coat of arms of Mauritius!
Dodos appear on coins from Mauritius.
Every Mauritius banknote has a hidden dodo watermark.
Mauritius became an independent country in 1968.
Sailors from Portugal visited Mauritius in 1507, but they didn't stay.
The Portuguese called Mauritius 'Swan Island.' Maybe the big dodos made them think of swans!
Dutch sailors wrote about dodos for the first time in 1598.
The first sailors to see dodos said they were bigger than swans.
The first picture of a dodo in a book was published in 1601.
Dutch sailors called the dodo 'walghvogel.' The name means 'tasteless bird.'
Some sailors called dodos 'dronte.' Some languages still use that name today!
Nobody knows for sure where the word 'dodo' comes from.
The word 'dodo' might copy the bird's call, which may have sounded like 'doo-doo.'
An English writer named Thomas Herbert first printed the word 'dodo' in 1634.
The dodo's science name is Raphus cucullatus.
'Cucullatus' means 'hooded.' The dodo's bare head looked like it wore a hood!
A famous scientist named Linnaeus once gave the dodo a name meaning 'silly dodo.'
Dodos were not afraid of people at all.
Dodos could bite hard with their big beaks!
Some sailors said dodo meat was tough or not tasty.
Live dodos were taken on ships to Europe and Asia.
At least eleven dodos reached faraway places alive.
In 1638, a live dodo was shown to visitors in London.
A dodo once lived in the zoo of an emperor in Prague.
Two live dodos were seen in India between 1628 and 1634.
A dodo was sent all the way to Nagasaki, Japan, in 1647, and it arrived alive!
The dodo in Japan was a gift. It was thought to be worth as much as a white deer.
The dodo sent to Japan is the last live dodo known to have been kept by people.
Long ago, a traveler named Peter Mundy wondered why dodos lived only on one island. That was 230 years before Charles Darwin's famous ideas!
Only about 20 pictures of dodos were made in the 1600s.
Sketches in the diary of a Dutch ship called the Gelderland are the only drawings made of dodos on Mauritius.
Roelant Savery painted dodos at least twelve times.
Savery's famous dodo painting from 1626 is in the Natural History Museum in London.
An old painting from India shows a slimmer, brownish dodo. Experts think it's one of the most accurate.
In 2009, an old dodo drawing sold for £44,450!
The last widely accepted sighting of a dodo was in 1662.
Dodos were probably all gone by about 1700.
Dodos died out less than 100 years after people found them.
People brought pigs, rats, cats, dogs, and monkeys to Mauritius.
Pigs and monkeys ate dodo eggs and took dodo food.
People cut down the forests where dodos lived.
Fewer than 50 people lived on Mauritius in the 1600s, but the animals they brought did a lot of damage.
Back then, many people didn't believe animals could go extinct.
Nobody noticed the dodo was gone for a long time.
After dodos disappeared, some people thought they were just a made-up story!
The dodo became a famous symbol of extinction.
People say 'dead as a dodo' to mean something is totally gone.
'Go the way of the dodo' means to disappear or become old-fashioned.
The dodo helped people realize that humans can cause animals to disappear forever.
Some later reports of 'dodos' were probably about the red rail bird.
Dodos survived volcanoes and climate changes for a very long time before people came.
Today, the dodo is used to help protect animals in danger, like at Durrell Wildlife Park.
Many other animals and plants on Mauritius went extinct after people arrived.
No complete stuffed dodo exists today.
The only dodo skin and soft parts left are a dried head and foot in Oxford, England.
A dodo skull is kept in a museum in Copenhagen, Denmark.
Part of a dodo skull is kept in the National Museum in Prague.
Stuffed 'dodos' in museums today are really made with feathers from other birds.
Many dodo bones were found in a swamp called the Mare aux Songes.
Mare aux Songes means 'pond of taro.'
In 1865, a schoolteacher named George Clark found lots of dodo bones in the swamp.
George Clark searched for dodo bones for 30 years!
Workers found dodo bones by feeling for them in the mud with their bare feet.
Bones from over 300 dodos came from the Mare aux Songes swamp.
Most dodo bones from the swamp are brown.
Dodos and other animals got stuck in the swamp during a long dry time about 4,200 years ago.
Most bones in the swamp came from giant tortoises, not dodos.
In 1904, the first complete skeleton of a single dodo was found in a cave near a mountain called Le Pouce.
In 2006, explorers found another dodo skeleton in a lava cave.
In 2005, scientists dug in the swamp again and found bones of at least 17 dodos.
26 museums around the world have important dodo bones.
Most dodo skeletons in museums are built from bones of several different dodos.
In 2011, a box of dodo bones was found in a London museum. It had been stored with crocodile bones!
Copies of the Oxford dodo head can be seen in many museums.
People say the Oxford museum burned its stuffed dodo, but that's a myth. It was put away to protect it.
The Oxford dodo was in the museum's collection by 1656.
Dodos were not as fat and clumsy as old paintings show.
Many old paintings showed overfed dodos from zoos or badly stuffed dodos.
Hunting was not the main reason dodos disappeared. The animals people brought were a bigger problem.
People once thought there was a white dodo on Réunion island. Scientists now know it was a mix-up with a white bird called an ibis.
No dodo bones have ever been found on Réunion.
Dodos were not stupid. They were probably as smart as pigeons.
Dodos were well suited to their island home.
A scientist in the 1860s built a dodo model that was too fat because he copied a painting. He fixed it later.
Many pictures of dodos are copies of older pictures, not drawings of real birds.
A dodo is a character in the book Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
Alice's Adventures in Wonderland came out in 1865.
The author of Alice, Lewis Carroll, made the Dodo character to stand for himself.
In Alice in Wonderland, the Dodo runs a silly race where everyone wins!
In the story, the Dodo gives Alice her own thimble as a prize.
Lewis Carroll and the real Alice liked to visit the dodo remains at the Oxford museum.
Alice in Wonderland made the dodo super famous.
The dodo is used as a mascot for lots of things in Mauritius.
